html:
District Six was a lively, mixed neighbourhood next to the centre of Cape Town. In 1966 the apartheid government declared it a white area, and over the next fifteen years about 60,000 residents were forced out and their homes bulldozed.

The district had grown in the 19th century as a home for freed slaves, workers, traders and immigrants. Most residents were Coloured, many of them Muslim Cape Malays, but black Africans, Indians, Jews and others lived there too. It was poor and crowded, but famous for its music, its carnival and its close community.

Under the Group Areas Act each racial group was assigned its own part of a city. District Six, near the harbour and city centre, was taken for whites. Families were moved to bleak new townships on the Cape Flats, far from work. Only churches and mosques were left standing. The removals echoed those at Sophiatown in Johannesburg in the 1950s.

The protests kept most of the land empty for decades. The District Six Museum opened in 1994, and after apartheid former residents began to claim the land back, though rebuilding has been slow.
